# README Articles & Presentations

Essential reading on the craft of writing great READMEs. Load these links when the user wants deeper guidance on README philosophy or best practices.

## Articles

- ["Art of Readme - Learn the art of writing quality READMEs."](https://github.com/hackergrrl/art-of-readme#readme) - *Stephen Whitmore* — foundational essay on what a README is for and how to write one that works.
- ["Elegant READMEs"](https://www.yegor256.com/2019/04/23/elegant-readme.html) - *Yegor Bugayenko* — argues for concision and structure over comprehensiveness.
- ["How To Write A Great README"](https://thoughtbot.com/blog/how-to-write-a-great-readme) - *Caleb Thompson (thoughtbot)* — practical, opinionated guide from a well-regarded consultancy.
- ["Readme Driven Development"](https://tom.preston-werner.com/2010/08/23/readme-driven-development.html) - *Tom Preston-Werner* — the case for writing your README before your code.
- ["Top ten reasons why I won't use your open source project"](https://changelog.com/posts/top-ten-reasons-why-i-wont-use-your-open-source-project) - *Adam Stacoviak* — failure modes to avoid; useful as a checklist.
- ["What I learned from an old GitHub project that won 3,000 Stars in a Week"](https://www.freecodecamp.org/news/what-i-learned-from-an-old-github-project-that-won-3-000-stars-in-a-week-628349a5ee14/) - *KyuWoo Choi* — what drives README virality.

## Architecture-specific Articles

- ["ARCHITECTURE.md"](https://matklad.github.io/2021/02/06/ARCHITECTURE.md.html) - *Alex Kladov* — strong argument for a dedicated architecture file in every non-trivial open-source project.
- ["Two open source projects with great documentation"](https://johnjago.com/great-docs/) - *John Jago* — concrete analysis of what makes documentation excellent.

## Presentations

- ["Build a Better README"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vfZuFo1gTB8&list=PLA9_Hq3zhoFw6patag2gZcDjpugDLBStL&index=31) - *Jason A. Crome* at *The Perl and Raku Conference* (2024, Las Vegas) — 30-minute talk covering structure, tone, and common mistakes.

## Key Takeaways

1. **Lead with the "why"** — users decide in seconds whether to continue reading. The first paragraph must answer: what does this do, and why should I care?
2. **Readme Driven Development** — write the README first; it forces clarity of intent before a line of code is written.
3. **Treat your README like a landing page** — it is often the first and only impression someone has of your project.
4. **One job per sentence** — avoid dense paragraphs. Lists, tables, and code blocks are your friends.
